description:
I'm an engineer working in energy innovation, applied R&D, and technology development. My background is in CCUS, renewables, project management and technology assessment.

I'm interested in exploring how change in environmental variables across different regions, can support better energy-related decisions.

I'm looking for

Python, data analysts

Earth science, climate data

Statistics, time-series, or NASA datasets

Web developers, data visualization 

Creative thinkers in UI/UX
summary:
Earth System Trend Detective is a web tool that lets anyone test whether a NASA Earth science variable is genuinely changing at a place they care about.

NASA publishes decades of Earth system data, but two things make it hard to use. There are far more variables than most people can navigate, and a variable can be rising in one place while it falls a few hundred kilometres away, so a single regional average may hide both signals at once.

The tool addresses both. You choose from 25 variables, each explained in one plain sentence, then click a point or drag a box on a world map. It fetches the monthly record live from NASA POWER, going back to 1981, removes the seasonal cycle, and runs three independent significance tests. It answers the challenge's four questions directly: what is changing, where, how much, and whether the change is statistically significant.

When a box is analysed, every NASA grid cell inside it is tested separately and drawn as a coloured dot. Over East Africa this reveals rainfall rising significantly in 88 cells and falling significantly in 29, inside a single region, which is exactly what a regional average would erase.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Earth System Trend Detective answers one question properly: is this Earth science variable, at this place, moving consistently in one direction, and can that be demonstrated rather than merely asserted?

The user picks a variable from twenty-five, grouped by subject (Heat, Water, Air, Sun and sky) rather than by the instrument or model that produced them, because someone investigating drought is unlikely to know which product contains soil moisture. Each variable carries a definition written in ordinary language, so root-zone soil wetness is introduced as the water available to plants in the top metre of soil. The user then clicks a point on a world map or drags a box of up to ten degrees, and receives a verdict: what is changing, where, by how much per decade, how much in total, and whether the change is statistically significant.

HOW IT WORKS

All data is requested live from the NASA POWER API at the moment of the query, with no key, no login and no cached copies. POWER serves monthly series from 1981 to the present, derived from NASA's MERRA-2 reanalysis and, for radiation variables, from NASA GEWEX/CERES, on a 0.5 by 0.625 degree grid. The tool calls the monthly/point endpoint for a single location and monthly/regional for a box.

The record is cleaned first, discarding POWER's month-13 annual summaries and its -999 fill values, and then deseasonalised by subtracting each calendar month's long-term mean. This step is essential rather than cosmetic: in Santiago the swing between summer and winter is roughly fourteen degrees while the trend is 0.17 C per decade, so the trend is entirely hidden inside the annual cycle until that cycle is removed.

Three independent tests are then applied. Ordinary least squares with a t-test gives the rate of change, a 95 per cent confidence interval and R squared. The Mann-Kendall test assumes nothing about the shape of the trend or the distribution of the data, asking only whether later values tend to exceed earlier ones, which makes it the more dependable test for a skewed variable such as precipitation. The Theil-Sen slope estimates the trend as the median of every pairwise slope in the record, so that a handful of extreme months cannot displace it.

THE CORRECTION THAT MATTERS MOST

Because conditions in one month are correlated with those in the month before, a record of 540 monthly values does not carry 540 independent pieces of evidence about the underlying trend. Testing it as though it did understates the standard error, with the result that almost any fluctuation is reported as significant. This is a common and quiet error. The tool estimates the lag-1 autocorrelation of the regression residuals and reduces the sample accordingly, to an effective n = n(1 - r1)/(1 + r1), following the approach of Santer et al. (2000), and runs the t-test on that reduced figure. For Amazon relative humidity this cuts 540 observations to an effective 76. Both r1 and the corrected sample size are displayed on screen rather than hidden, and the tool warns the user when what remains is too small to carry weight.

For a box, every grid cell is analysed separately and drawn as a coloured dot, ringed in white where that cell is individually significant. The area-averaged series is weighted by the cosine of latitude. A ten-degree box contains up to 357 cells and is analysed in under a second.

VERIFICATION

The statistics engine was checked against SciPy and pymannkendall on six synthetic series covering a clean trend, pure noise, skewed and tied data, a short record, a strongly autocorrelated series, and a series with missing values. Every quantity, including the OLS slope, standard error, t, p, R squared, Mann-Kendall S, var(S), Z and tau, and the Theil-Sen slope, agrees to within one part in a billion. Two genuine defects were found and corrected through this process. Every worked example built into the tool was then run against live NASA data, so the figures it quotes are real results rather than illustrations.

INTENDED IMPACT

The tool is aimed at secondary and university students, and at anyone with some scientific background who wants to check something for themselves. It is built to encourage three habits. Remove the seasonal cycle before looking for a trend, which the interface lets you toggle so the difference is visible. Treat a trend as a claim that must be tested, and note that three tests which disagree are telling you something real about your data. Finally, accept that "not significant" is an honest answer: one built-in example, London rainfall at p = 0.51, exists precisely to demonstrate that finding nothing is a finding, and that some trends only emerge with a longer record.

TOOLS AND APPROACH

The tool is one self-contained HTML file written in plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no frameworks, no build step and no external libraries or CDNs. This was a deliberate decision rather than a limitation: there is no build to reproduce and nothing that can change underneath it, so the page should continue working unaltered for as long as the NASA POWER API does. The world map is drawn on HTML canvas in an equirectangular projection from a simplified Natural Earth coastline embedded in the file, so the map needs no tile server and makes no external request. Charts are generated as inline SVG. The statistics are implemented from scratch in JavaScript, including the log-gamma function, the incomplete beta function for the t-distribution, and the complementary error function for the normal distribution. Verification was carried out in Python using SciPy, NumPy and pymannkendall.

LIMITATIONS WE CHOSE TO STATE

The tool fits linear trends. Real Earth system change can be non-linear, can shift abruptly, and can be driven by cycles such as ENSO that are not removed here. A significant linear trend is evidence of consistent directional change over the chosen period; it is not a forecast and it does not establish a cause. This is stated in the interface itself rather than left for the user to discover.
